prompt: Sort each analysis by whether the level of measurement of its data permits it.

bins.label: Assumes a higher level than the data possess

cards.text: Reporting the store format (supermarket, convenience store, online) that respondents use most often.
cards.explanation: Store format is nominal, and nominal data permit counts, percentages and the mode.

cards.text: Reporting that the average respondent identification number in the sample is 512.4.
cards.explanation: Identification numbers are nominal labels. A mean assumes at least interval data and cannot be meaningfully interpreted.

cards.text: Reporting the median rank that respondents gave a coffee brand among five brands.
cards.explanation: Ranks are ordinal, and ordinal data permit the median and percentiles.

cards.text: Concluding that the brand ranked first is preferred twice as much as the brand ranked second.
cards.explanation: Ranks show order but not the magnitude of the differences, so statements of proportion are not permitted.

cards.text: Reporting the mean and standard deviation of ratings of a hotel on a scale from 1 to 7.
cards.explanation: Rating scales are commonly treated as interval scales, which permit the mean and the standard deviation.

cards.text: Concluding that a day of 30 degrees Celsius is twice as warm as a day of 15 degrees Celsius.
cards.explanation: Celsius is an interval scale with an arbitrary zero, so 30 degrees is not twice as warm as 15 degrees.

cards.text: Concluding that loyalty-card members spend three times as much per month as non-members.
cards.explanation: Spending has an absolute zero point, so it is a ratio scale and statements of proportion are permitted.

prompt: Each case describes a survey item. Name the scaling technique it uses.

cases.text: Respondents mark a point between “punctual” and “unpunctual,” and between “uncomfortable” and “comfortable,” for an airline.
cases.explanation: Pairs of opposite adjectives at the two ends of a scale, with the favorable adjective on different sides: a semantic differential scale.

cases.text: Respondents divide 100 points among battery life, camera, price and screen size to show how much each matters.
cases.explanation: A fixed number of points divided among attributes to show their relative importance: a constant sum scale.

cases.text: Respondents rate “The staff at this gym are helpful” from 1, strongly disagree, to 7, strongly agree.
cases.explanation: A statement rated by degree of agreement, evaluated on its own: a Likert scale.

cases.text: Respondents taste two orange juices and state which one they prefer.
cases.explanation: A choice of one of two objects according to a criterion: a paired comparison scale.

cases.text: Respondents place six streaming services in order from the one they would keep longest to the one they would cancel first.
cases.explanation: Several objects placed in order by a criterion: a rank-order scale.

cases.text: Respondents rate a bank on seven-point scales between “traditional” and “innovative,” and between “trustworthy” and “untrustworthy.”
cases.explanation: Opposite adjectives at the ends of a seven-point scale, used to describe the image of a company: a semantic differential scale.

prompt: Each case describes a change to a rating scale. Name the decision the researcher has made.

cases.text: A survey about a new pension product adds “I don’t know enough to say,” because many employees have not read the plan.
cases.explanation: A “don’t know” option makes the scale nonforced, which suits respondents who lack the knowledge to answer.

cases.text: A researcher replaces a five-point scale with a six-point scale, so that respondents cannot choose the middle.
cases.explanation: An even number of categories removes the neutral midpoint and requires respondents to lean in one direction.

cases.text: A hotel’s scale reads poor, good, very good, excellent, outstanding: one unfavorable category and four favorable ones.
cases.explanation: The favorable and unfavorable categories are unequal in number, so the scale is unbalanced.

cases.text: A scale from 1 to 7 carries words only at 1, “very dissatisfied,” and at 7, “very satisfied.”
cases.explanation: Labels are provided only for the endpoints rather than for every category.

cases.text: A researcher reduces a scale from twenty points to seven, because respondents cannot reliably tell point 14 from point 15.
cases.explanation: Respondents can reliably distinguish only a limited number of categories; five to nine are commonly used.

prompt: Sort each measure by what it achieves.

cards.text: A tape measure whose first five centimeters have been cut off, so every length it gives is five centimeters too long.
cards.explanation: Its readings are consistent, so it is reliable, but they are systematically wrong, so it is not valid.

cards.text: A satisfaction item worded so that it consistently encourages favorable answers, and gives the same results each time it is repeated.
cards.explanation: Consistent results show reliability; the systematic error of the wording means the item is not valid.

cards.text: A published service-quality scale that gives consistent results over time and correlates with other measures of service quality.
cards.explanation: Consistent results show reliability, and convergent evidence supports its validity.

cards.text: An item answered at the end of a long questionnaire, when fatigued respondents give very different answers each time it is repeated.
cards.explanation: Inconsistent results mean the item is not reliable, and a measure cannot be valid without being reliable.

cards.text: A kitchen scale that gives the correct weight of a bag of flour every time.
cards.explanation: Its readings are consistent and correct: free of both random and systematic error.

cards.text: A thermometer whose readings of the same room jump by several degrees from one minute to the next.
cards.explanation: Its readings vary unpredictably, so it is not reliable, and therefore it cannot be valid.

prompt: Each draft question breaks one wording principle. Name the problem.

cases.text: “How satisfied are you with the speed and the cost of our delivery?”
cases.explanation: It asks about two issues at once, so one answer cannot show which one the respondent means.
“Regularly” may mean weekly to one respondent and yearly to another.

cases.text: “Wouldn’t you agree that our loyalty program offers excellent value?”
cases.explanation: The wording suggests the desired answer.

cases.text: “How would you rate our omnichannel fulfillment proposition?”
cases.explanation: “Omnichannel fulfillment proposition” is a technical term that respondents may not understand.

cases.text: “How many times a week do you use the app’s budgeting feature?” asked of every customer.
cases.explanation: It assumes that the respondent uses the feature without first establishing it.

cases.text: “Which brand of shampoo did you buy in March three years ago?”
cases.explanation: Respondents cannot accurately recall a distant purchase; recent purchases are asked instead.

prompt: Match each form of response bias with the case that shows it.

pairs.match: Respondents report twice as many hours of exercise per week as their fitness trackers record.
pairs.explanation: Overstating a behavior that presents the respondent favorably is social desirability bias.

pairs.match: A respondent agrees both that the store is too expensive and that the store is good value.
pairs.explanation: Agreeing with two contradictory statements shows agreement regardless of content.

pairs.match: A respondent answers every rating question with a 1 or a 7, whatever the question asks.
pairs.explanation: Selecting the endpoints of the scale regardless of the question is extreme responding.

pairs.match: A respondent selects 4 on every seven-point item in a long online survey.
pairs.explanation: Selecting the middle of the scale regardless of the question is midpoint responding.

pairs.match: Customers rate the shop’s service more favorably when the interviewer wears the shop’s uniform.
pairs.explanation: The presence or behavior of the interviewer influences the responses.

prompt: A research team needs a scale to measure trust in a food-delivery app. Put the steps of the procedure in order.

steps.text: The team writes a definition of trust in a delivery app in words.
steps.explanation: The construct is first defined conceptually.

steps.text: The team searches published research for an existing validated trust scale that suits the study.
steps.explanation: A suitable validated scale is used in its published form; items are generated only if none exists.

steps.text: Finding no suitable scale, the team asks an AI tool for thirty candidate items.
steps.explanation: AI generates the pool of candidate items only after the search for a validated scale.

steps.text: Three experts review the items for coverage of the construct and for flaws in wording.
steps.explanation: Experts judge content validity and wording before any pretesting.

steps.text: AI-simulated respondents answer the revised items and flag obvious ambiguities.
steps.explanation: AI pretesting comes before real respondents and supplements them.

steps.text: Twelve app users explain aloud how they interpret each item in cognitive interviews.
steps.explanation: Pretesting with real respondents reveals the problems that AI-simulated respondents cannot.

steps.text: The scale is administered to a pilot sample, and its reliability and validity are assessed.
steps.explanation: The procedure ends with the assessment of reliability and validity in a pilot sample.

question_text: A research team wants to measure the price consciousness of three language models that a retailer is considering as shopping assistants. A validated eight-item price-consciousness scale exists. Which procedure follows the approach introduced on this slide?
hint: Consider the form of the scale, how the items are presented, and how the model is asked to answer.
correct_answer_citation: Week 04 · Measuring the Attitudes of AI Models

options.option_text: Ask each model, in an open-ended question, how important low prices are to it, and code the answers.
options.option_explanation: Open-ended answers from a model can be evasive, and they do not use the validated measure.

options.option_text: Shorten the scale to the three items that seem most relevant to AI, and present them together in one prompt.
options.option_explanation: Changing the scale removes its established reliability and validity, and the items are administered separately.

options.option_text: Administer all eight items in their exact validated wording, each in a separate prompt, with a fixed instruction to answer with a single scale point.
options.option_explanation: Correct. The exact validated form retains the measure's reliability and validity, and the fixed instruction prevents evasive answers.

options.option_text: Ask each model to rate its own price consciousness on a single seven-point item.
options.option_explanation: A single self-rating is not the validated multi-item scale used for consumers.
